Meta Tags Explained

What Are Meta Tags & Why Do They Matter?

Meta tags are HTML snippets in your page's head that tell search engines and social platforms what your page is about.

Title Tag

The most important on-page SEO element. Appears as the clickable blue link in Google results. Keep it 50–60 characters, include your primary keyword near the start. Every page needs a unique title tag.

Meta Description

The grey text under your title in Google results. Doesn't directly affect rankings but massively affects click-through rate. Keep it 120–160 characters with a clear benefit and call to action.

Open Graph Tags

Control how your page looks when shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. Without OG tags, social platforms guess — and usually get it wrong. Add an og:image for dramatically higher engagement on social shares.

Twitter Cards

Twitter uses its own card system separate from Open Graph. The "summary_large_image" card shows a big image above your tweet — much more engaging than plain text links and increases click-through significantly.

Robots Meta Tag

Tells search engine crawlers what to do with the page. "index, follow" (default) means crawl and index. Use "noindex" for thank-you pages, staging sites, or admin pages you don't want in search results.

SEO Best Practices

Every page needs a unique title and description. Include your target keyword naturally in the title. Write descriptions that compel clicks, not just keyword stuffing. Update OG tags whenever you share content on social.

Meta Tags FAQ

Common Questions

Do meta keywords still matter for SEO?+

No. Google officially stopped using the meta keywords tag in 2009. Bing and most other search engines also ignore it. You can include it for internal tracking purposes, but it has no effect on your rankings.

How long should my meta description be?+

Google typically displays 120–160 characters of a meta description in search results. Longer descriptions get cut off with "...". Write the most important information first. Google may also rewrite your description if it thinks something else on the page is more relevant.

What size should my OG image be?+

The recommended Open Graph image size is 1200×630 pixels (a 1.91:1 ratio). This displays correctly on Facebook, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. For Twitter large image cards, 1200×628px works well. Keep file size under 1MB for fast loading.

Can I use the same meta description on multiple pages?+

Technically yes, but you shouldn't. Duplicate meta descriptions are a missed opportunity — each page should have a unique description that accurately describes that specific page's content. This also helps Google understand your site structure.

Why is Google showing a different description than mine?+

Google may rewrite your meta description if it determines that content from the page itself better answers the search query. This is normal. Focus on making your page content strong and write a compelling description — Google will usually use it for branded searches.
